title: The Not-So-Secret To Effective Classroom Management anagement/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin observes that many struggling teachers cycle endlessly through new strategies -- bulletin boards, chants, attention-getting devices, community circles -- only to fall back on lecturing, yelling, and office referrals when these novelties fail to work. He argues that while none of these tools are inherently bad, they are missing a widely-known but rarely practiced ingredient: near-universal, exact follow-through on stated rules and consequences. He notes that while almost all teachers have rules and consequences in place, only a small percentage actually enforce them consistently and precisely every time, and that this gap -- not the specific techniques chosen -- is the real reason so many classroom management plans fail. He proposes a concrete experiment: for one day, enforce a single rule (such as no calling out) with total consistency, and use the resulting volume of consequences as diagnostic information about how loosely the plan had actually been enforced before. He anticipates that students may initially react with shock or resistance to sudden strict enforcement, and recommends restarting with a full review, explanation, and role-play of the plan if so, along with daily review for the first four to six weeks of a school year. He closes by tying consistent enforcement to reduced need for lecturing, arguing, or raising one's voice.
points: Teachers often chase new engagement gimmicks (bulletin boards, chants, attention-getters) while overlooking the real, well-known ingredient of effective classroom management: exact, consistent follow-through.
Only a small percentage of teachers who have rules and consequences in place actually enforce them precisely every single time, which is identified as the central reason plans fail.
A proposed diagnostic experiment: enforce one rule with total consistency for a day and use the resulting number of consequences to gauge how loosely the plan had previously been enforced.
If students react with shock or resistance to strict enforcement, the recommendation is to restart the plan from scratch with review, explanation, and role-play.
Reviewing the classroom management plan daily for the first four to six weeks of the school year, then weekly thereafter, is recommended to sustain consistency.
quotes: They test drive interactive bulletin boards, ever-new sets of rules and consequences, echoing chants, bells, and other attention-getting devices, and time-consuming community circles.

99% of teachers have rules or standards of behavior for their classroom, and most of these teachers have consequences in case these rules are broken. This is good. But here is the problem: only a small percentage of teachers actually follow their rules and consequences to the letter.
The central reason why so many teachers struggle with classroom management is because they don’t really follow their plan. Most only kinda-sorta do.

Every time you let something go, ignore a broken rule, or fail to enforce a rule with a consequence, you are letting your students know that you don’t really mean what you say, that you can’t be counted on or trusted.
In the beginning of the school year or if you’re starting over, it’s a good idea to review your plan daily for the first four to six weeks.

And here is the best part: it’s not personal. Because you’re following your plan and delivering on the promise you gave your students, there will be no more need for less effective and potentially hurtful methods like lecturing, arguing, or raising your voice.
